newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Key road reopens in Indonesia's troubled Kalimantan.
newsitem.headline: Key road reopens in Indonesia's troubled Kalimantan.

text.p: Indonesian police said on Sunday a key road through the interior of jungle-covered West Kalimantan province was reopened at the weekend after it was blocked by troops during widespread ethnic unrest.
"The road to Pontianak is open," a policeman, who declined to be identified, told Reuters by telephone from Sanggau, 140 km (87 miles) east of the regional capital.
The policeman would not give any further information, but residents said on Sunday that public announcements were made by loudspeaker saying the road was now open.

Church sources from the province said on Sunday the unrest between local Dayak tribesmen and migrants from Madura island off Java had cut a swathe across West Kalimantan from Singkawang on the west coast to Sintang, about 300 km (186 miles) inland.
The neighbouring Malaysian state of Sarawak closed its borders a week ago as the unrest flared.

Last weekend, the army moved about 200 troops from neighbouring East Kalimantan province to reinforce those manning heavily-armed road blocks stopping traffic to and from the interior's few main thoroughfares.
Tensions exploded on New Year's Day when about 5,000 Dayak tribesmen rioted in Sanggau Ledo, 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak, attacking the Madurese. At least five died.
The military has reported casualties from fighting as recent as Friday but the authorities have declined to give a detailed account of the problems or the number of dead and injured.

Residents and church sources said they knew of at least seven dead in two separate incidents in Sanggau and Tebas, about 150 km (93 miles) north of Pontianak, but police said injuries were light in what they described as a "social problem".
Residents say the attacks have included assaults by large groups of Dayaks on military installations housing Madurese refugees.
The indigenous Dayaks are often Christian and the Madurese Moslem in mostly Islamic Indonesia, where various ethnic and religious riots have left at least 12 people dead since October.
Marzuki Darusman, deputy chairman of the official National Commission on Human Rights, said on Saturday the commission was monitoring the situation but had not yet decided to send a team.
